title: Myanmar — Tatmadaw sexual violence against Rohingya and ethnic minority women, girls and boys (UN FFM)
who: Myanmar armed forces (Tatmadaw)
what: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. It documented Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, detained at Buthidaung prison in 2012 and subjected to sexual violence.

title: Sudan — RSF rape and sexual slavery of women and girls (UN Fact-Finding Mission 2024)
who: Rapid Support Forces and allied militias; also some cases by Sudanese Armed Forces
what: The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan found that rape and gang rape were widespread, mostly by men in RSF uniform and allied militias, with victims including girls as young as 8. It found the abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes by the RSF amounted to sexual slavery. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023 (RSF 57) and 74 children in 2024 (RSF 54, RSF-affiliated militia 9) and listed the RSF for rape and abduction of children.

title: Ethiopia — Tigray war sexual violence including girls (ICHREE; UN verified)
who: Ethiopian National Defence Forces, Eritrean Defence Forces, Amhara forces and Tigrayan forces
what: The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (October 2022) documented Tigrayan forces' rapes of women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages such as Chenna in 2021, alongside widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray. BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at Mekelle health facilities as rape survivors. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024, 38 attributed to the ENDF.

title: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
who: Russian armed forces and authorities
network: Russian state system for transfer, adoption and 're-education' of Ukrainian children
what: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.

title: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
network: Russian state system for transfer, adoption and 're-education' of Ukrainian children
what: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.

title: China — Uyghur children separated from detained parents and placed in state boarding schools
who: Chinese state authorities in Xinjiang
what: As hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the BBC reported in July 2019, with research by Adrian Zenz, a rapid campaign to build boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitory space, including $1.2bn spent in southern Xinjiang; records showed more than 400 children in one township had lost both parents to internment or prison, and children were assessed for 'centralised care'. School rules imposed points-based punishments on pupils and teachers for speaking anything other than Chinese. Zenz found evidence that children of detainees were being channelled into the boarding system in large numbers. The New York Times reported in December 2019 that about 497,000 pupils were enrolled in such schools. A Xinjiang propaganda official denied that the state was caring for large numbers of parentless children. No sexual-abuse finding is recorded here;

title: Okinawa — rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen (1995)
who: US Navy and Marine Corps personnel from Camp Hansen
what: In September 1995 three US servicemen based on Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl. They were tried in a Japanese court and in 1996 were each found guilty and sentenced to between six years and six months and seven years in prison. The case triggered mass protests against the US bases.

title: Bosnia — Foča rape camps; ICTY Kunarac judgment (girls as young as 12 enslaved)
who: Bosnian Serb army (VRS) and paramilitaries; local police chief named in testimony
what: In Serb-held Foča in 1992–93, Bosniak women and girls were held at detention sites such as Partizan Sports Hall, next to the municipal police building, and taken from there to apartments and private houses to be raped; the ICTY found rape was used by Bosnian Serb forces as an instrument of terror and that local police guarded the women and joined in their mistreatment. On 22 February 2001 the ICTY sentenced Dragoljub Kunarac, a VRS reconnaissance unit leader, to 28 years for torture, rape and enslavement; Radomir Kovač to 20 years for enslavement, rape and outrages upon personal dignity, including detaining two girls in his apartment for about four months and selling victims to other soldiers; and Zoran Vuković to 12 years for torture and rape, including raping a girl he knew to be 15. The sentences were upheld on appeal on 12 June 2002.

title: Israel/Gaza — UN COI findings on sexual violence incl. against Palestinian boys and on 7 October
who: Israeli security forces (detention and arrest); Hamas and other armed groups (7 October)
what: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that 'men and boys were targeted in particular ways'; it found gender persecution of Palestinian men and boys as a crime against humanity. It also found sexual violence was committed on 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, Nahal Oz and several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage. Recorded only to the extent of these UN findings.

title: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
what: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria; thousands remain missing.

title: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
who: Boko Haram (JAS)
what: On the night of 14 April 2014 Boko Haram gunmen raided the dormitories of the Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno state, and loaded 276 girls onto trucks; more than 50 escaped within hours, mostly by jumping off the lorries, leaving 219 in captivity, some later found in the Sambisa Forest. Amnesty International said on the tenth anniversary in April 2024 that 82 girls remained in captivity and that 20 released girls had been forced to marry former Boko Haram fighters; in April 2015 it estimated that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since the start of 2014.

title: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
what: On the evening of 19 February 2018 militants stormed Dapchi, Yobe state, and abducted girls from a boarding school; Nigeria's government said 110 schoolgirls were missing. On 21 March 2018 the government said 106 children — 104 schoolgirls, a girl who did not attend the school and a boy — had been freed, and denied paying a ransom. Five girls were reported to have died during the journey after the abduction. The only Christian girl in the group, who refused to convert, remained in captivity.

title: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
what: On the night of Friday 11 December 2020 heavily armed gunmen raided the all-boys Government Science Secondary School in Kankara, Katsina state, where more than 800 students lived. The military said 333 pupils were unaccounted for. In an audio message a man identifying himself as Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction; Nigerian officials attributed it to bandits, and the BBC later described a local gang leader as the mastermind of the kidnapping of about 300 boys. The boys were freed within about a week.

title: Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024)
who: Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'Awati Wal-Jihad (JAS/Boko Haram), ISWAP, Bakura
what: The UN verified the abduction of 991 children (354 boys, 637 girls) in Nigeria in 2024 by JAS (690), ISWAP (294) and Bakura (7), most for recruitment and use. It also verified sexual violence, all involving forced marriage, against 419 children (7 boys, 412 girls) by JAS (304), ISWAP (114) and Bakura (1). In 2023 the UN had verified sexual violence against 366 children following abduction.

title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

title: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
who: Lord's Resistance Army commanders Lt. Col. Binansio Okumu ('Binany') and 'Obol', reporting to Gen. Dominic Ongwen (per HRW)
what: From 14 to 17 December 2009 Lord's Resistance Army forces attacked at least 10 villages in the remote Makombo area of Haute-Uélé, north-eastern DR Congo, killing at least 321 civilians and abducting 250 others, including at least 80 children. Human Rights Watch, which documented the previously unreported massacre after a field mission in February 2010, said it was carried out by two LRA commanders who reported to Gen. Dominic Ongwen, the senior LRA leader believed to command its forces in Congo and wanted by the International Criminal Court.

title: Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07)
who: Former FARC-EP secretariat and commanders
what: The Special Jurisdiction for Peace's Case 07 investigates the recruitment and use of children by the former FARC-EP; in August 2021 it identified a provisional universe of 18,677 unique victims and has accredited 9,854. The JEP indicted former FARC-EP commanders for war crimes including the recruitment and use of children and sexual violence against children, and has referred a former FARC member accused of reproductive violence against recruited girls to its investigation unit. Former secretariat members have publicly acknowledged responsibility.

title: Haiti — armed gangs' sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024)
who: Viv Ansanm gang coalition (411 cases) and other armed gangs
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children (523 girls, 43 boys) in Haiti in 2024, 411 attributed to the Viv Ansanm coalition; cases involved rape (406) and gang rape (160). This was up from 41 girls verified in 2023. Viv Ansanm was listed in the Secretary-General's annex for rape and other sexual violence against children, recruitment, killing and maiming, and attacks on schools and hospitals.

title: Somalia — Al-Shabaab abduction and sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024)
who: Al-Shabaab; also Somali National Army, police, Ethiopian Liyu Police, clan militias
what: The UN verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia in 2024, 850 by Al-Shabaab, mainly for recruitment. It verified sexual violence against 267 children (265 girls): Al-Shabaab 120, unidentified 110, government security forces 14 (Somali National Army 11), Ethiopian Liyu Police 7. The Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

title: Mozambique, Cabo Delgado — abduction of children by ISIS-linked armed groups
who: Islamic State–Mozambique Province ('Al-Shabaab' locally) and other armed groups; also Mozambique defence forces (sexual violence, 2023)
what: The UN verified the abduction of 468 children (371 boys, 97 girls) by armed groups in Cabo Delgado in 2024, 392 for recruitment, and sexual violence against 5 girls. In 2023 it verified 92 abductions (4 for sexual violence) and sexual violence against 12 girls attributed to the Mozambique Defence Armed Forces (5), armed groups (4) and the police Rapid Intervention Unit (3).

title: DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024)
who: M23 (68), CODECO (63), FARDC (47), Raia Mutomboki, Nyatura, ADF and others
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC in 2024, by M23 (68), CODECO (63), the Armed Forces of the DRC (47), Raia Mutomboki (33), Nyatura (24) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, by ADF (265), M23 (178) and others. In 2022 it verified sexual violence against 284 children aged 4 to 17, 56 of them by FARDC.

title: Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024)
who: CPC coalition (UPC, 3R, anti-balaka); national defence forces; Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe; RSF
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in CAR in 2024: CPC armed groups 58, government and pro-government forces 35 (national defence forces 21, Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe 9), PRNC 11, Sudanese RSF 2. It verified the abduction of 141 children, most for recruitment and/or sexual violence. The Secretary-General said he was deeply concerned by rising violations by government and pro-government forces.

title: South Sudan — sexual violence against girls by SSPDF and other forces (UN verified)
who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF), SPLM/A-IO factions, police
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls, as young as 7, in South Sudan in 2022, 74 of them by the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, plus SPLM/A-IO Kit-Gwang (10), SPLM/A-IO (4) and the National Police Service (2). In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 7 girls, 5 by the SSPDF.

title: Mali — UN-verified rape and abduction of children (2022–2024)
who: JNIM, ISGS, Malian armed forces, foreign security personnel and others
what: The UN verified the rape of 32 girls in Mali in 2024 by unidentified perpetrators (22), ISGS (4), JNIM (3), the Malian armed forces (2) and Ganda Lassal Izo (1), and the abduction of 119 children, including 4 by foreign security personnel. In 2023 it verified the rape of 15 girls, 4 by the Malian armed forces.

title: Burkina Faso — abduction of children by JNIM, ISGS and state auxiliaries (UN verified)
who: JNIM, ISGS, Defence and Security Forces / Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP)
what: The UN verified the abduction of 309 children in Burkina Faso in 2024 by JNIM (157), ISGS (80), unidentified perpetrators (47) and the Defence and Security Forces/VDP (25), and the rape of four girls, two by the VDP. In 2022 it verified the rape of 16 girls, 2 by the Defence and Security Forces.

title: Niger — UN-verified abduction of children (2023–2024)
who: JAS, ISWAP, ISGS, unidentified perpetrators; Niger security forces (one case 2023)
what: The UN verified the abduction of 202 children (102 girls) in Niger in 2024 by unidentified perpetrators (163), JAS (35), ISWAP (2) and ISGS (2), and sexual violence against five girls. In 2023 it verified sexual violence against 8 girls, one by the Niger security forces.

title: Cameroon — sexual violence against girls by armed forces and JAS (UN verified 2023)
who: Cameroon Armed Forces; JAS; unidentified perpetrators
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon in 2023, 10 attributed to the Cameroon Armed Forces, 6 to unidentified perpetrators and 1 to JAS. In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 6 girls (1 by the armed forces) and the abduction of 50 children.

title: Yemen — sexual violence against children by government-affiliated forces and Houthis (UN verified)
who: Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (police, Security Belt, Amaliqah); Houthis
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 24 children (8 boys, 16 girls) in Yemen in 2023, 20 attributed to the Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (Yemen Armed Forces 9, Yemeni police 4). In 2024 it verified 11 cases (6 boys, 5 girls), attributed to the Houthis (2), Yemen Armed Forces (2) and affiliated forces (7), including Yemeni police (4).

title: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified)
who: Taliban de facto authorities
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 12 children (6 boys, 6 girls) in Afghanistan in 2023, 10 attributed to the Taliban, and the abduction of 3 children by the Taliban for sexual violence purposes. It verified 13 cases in 2022 (Taliban 7) and 6 in 2024 (Taliban 5).

title: Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified)
who: ELN, FARC-EP dissident groups, Clan del Golfo; Colombian armed forces (2 cases 2023)
what: The UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in Colombia in 2024, by the ELN (12), FARC-EP dissident groups (12), Clan del Golfo (7) and unidentified perpetrators. In 2023 it verified 26 cases, including 2 by the Colombian armed forces.

title: Myanmar — abduction of children by armed forces and armed groups (UN verified)
who: Myanmar armed forces and Pyu Saw Htee; KIA; MNDAA; PDFs
what: The UN verified the abduction of 85 children in Myanmar in 2024, 41 by the Myanmar armed forces and affiliated militias and 33 by the KIA, mostly for recruitment; it verified the rape of 2 girls (Myanmar armed forces 1, KIA 1).

title: Syria — abduction of children by armed groups and government forces (UN verified)
who: Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, Syrian government forces, YPG/YPJ
what: The UN verified the abduction of 14 children (5 boys, 9 girls) in Syria in 2024 by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement (9), Syrian government forces (4) and YPG/YPJ (1), often for recruitment and use.

title: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cover_up: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them.
what: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.

title: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity
who: Kincora staff (William McGrath, Raymond Semple, Joseph Mains — convicted 1981); alleged: MI5, army intelligence, RUC Special Branch
cover_up: Abuse allegations reached the RUC by 1977 without prosecution until 1980; the Hart inquiry found a 'catalogue of failures' by police and authorities. Former army officers Colin Wallace and Brian Gemmell said in 2014 that superiors stopped them passing on or pursuing information.
what: Three Kincora staff were convicted in 1981 of systematic sexual abuse of boys in their care. For decades it was alleged that McGrath, leader of the loyalist group Tara, was an MI5 agent and that intelligence services protected a ring of prominent abusers to blackmail them. On 20 January 2017 the Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart found 'no credible evidence' that others were involved or that 'the security agencies were complicit in any form of sexual abuse in Kincora for any purpose', and said the 'honey pot' blackmail claim was without foundation; it said the government's promise to hand over all files had been honoured. In June 2025 former resident Gary Hoy settled his civil claim against the PSNI and Home Secretary, which alleged McGrath was protected as an MI5 agent, on confidential terms with no admission of liability.

title: Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined
who: Government of Quebec under Maurice Duplessis; Catholic religious orders running orphanages and hospitals
cover_up: No criminal charges resulted from the 1990s complaints; the 2001 compensation excluded victims of sexual or other abuse.
what: Under Premier Maurice Duplessis, many poor or illegitimate children in Quebec who were not mentally ill were sent in the 1940s and 1950s to church-run psychiatric institutions so that the orphanages could qualify for extra federal aid; Wikipedia, citing historians, gives subsidies of $2.75 a day for psychiatric patients against $1.25 for orphans. Survivors say they were beaten, sexually abused, and subjected to electroshock and lobotomies. Premier Lucien Bouchard apologised in 1999. In July 2001 the orphans accepted Quebec's final offer of $10,000 per person plus $1,000 for each year of wrongful confinement, about $25,000 each, not covering sexual or other abuse; about 3,000 were then still alive. Claims linking the orphans to CIA MKUltra experiments are not established by the sources consulted.

title: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
what: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.

title: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children
who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC/FPLC)
what: On 14 March 2012 the ICC found Thomas Lubanga guilty of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him on 10 July 2012 to 14 years; the verdict was confirmed on 1 December 2014. Sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but not charged. He was released on 15 March 2020 after serving his sentence.

title: Al Hassan (Ansar Eddine, Timbuktu) — ICC: convicted of torture/persecution; acquitted of rape and sexual slavery
who: Ansar Eddine / AQIM Islamic police in Timbuktu
what: On 26 June 2024 the ICC convicted Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz of crimes against humanity and war crimes including torture and persecution in Timbuktu, but acquitted him of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery (charges that included forced marriages of women and girls). Recorded here as an acquittal on the sexual-violence counts only.

title: Ukraine — UN-verified abduction of children by Russian armed forces and authorities (2022–2023)
who: Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied territories
network: Russian state system for transfer, adoption and 're-education' of Ukrainian children
what: The UN Secretary-General verified the abduction, beginning in 2022 and continuing into 2023, of 122 children (75 boys, 47 girls) attributed to Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories; 91 abductions by Russian armed forces had been verified for 2022. The 2025 report welcomed the reunification of two of these children and said the whereabouts of the rest remained unknown.

title: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site
who: Staff named from IOM, MSF, WFP, World Vision and others in a UN-run camp
what: A September 2022 investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers in the UN-run Malakal Protection of Civilians site exploited displaced women and girls, including 'sex for aid'; women and girls reported being raped and becoming pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named.

title: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022)
who: Chadian National Army
what: The UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and in Sudan attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to the Chadian National Army. In the Lake Chad basin it verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa.

title: Iraq — abduction of children by Da'esh and HPG/PKK (UN verified 2022–2024)
who: Da'esh; HPG/PKK
what: The UN verified the abduction of 18 children in Iraq in 2022, 10 by Da'esh and 4 by HPG/PKK, and of 8 children in 2024 (2 boys by Da'esh, 6 girls by HPG/PKK), mostly for recruitment and use.

title: Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge
who: Jeffrey Epstein (financier)
cover_up: Police chief Michael Reiter said state prosecutors under State Attorney Barry Krischer grew dismissive about six months in; he asked Krischer to step aside. The July 2006 state grand jury returned only one felony solicitation-of-prostitution count. Reiter then referred the case to the FBI.
what: In March 2005 a woman told Palm Beach police her 14-year-old stepdaughter had been paid to give Epstein a massage at his mansion. A 13-month police investigation identified about 35 girls. In July 2006 a state grand jury returned a single count of felony solicitation of prostitution and Epstein was arrested on 23 July 2006. Reiter later called the outcome 'the worst failure of the criminal justice system' in modern times.

title: Epstein — 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 state plea
who: Jeffrey Epstein; US Attorney's Office, Southern District of Florida (Alexander Acosta)
cover_up: Lenient deal: the federal non-prosecution agreement (2007) dropped federal charges against Epstein and 'several suspected co-conspirators' in return for a state guilty plea; it was kept from victims. Epstein served 13 months of an 18-month term, much of it on daily work release. In Feb 2019 Judge Kenneth Marra ruled prosecutors violated the Crime Victims' Rights Act by not telling victims while ur
what: After the FBI opened a federal probe, US Attorney Alexander Acosta's office negotiated a non-prosecution agreement in 2007. On 30 June 2008 Epstein pleaded guilty in Palm Beach County to soliciting prostitution and soliciting a minor; he was sentenced to 18 months, registered as a sex offender and was released on 22 July 2009 after 13 months. A 2018 Miami Herald series (Julie K. Brown) identified 80 victims and reopened scrutiny. Acosta resigned as US Labor Secretary in July 2019.

title: Epstein — 2019 federal sex-trafficking indictment and death in custody
who: Jeffrey Epstein; Metropolitan Correctional Center (Bureau of Prisons)
cover_up: DOJ Inspector General (June 2023) found negligence and misconduct by Bureau of Prisons staff: 13 employees showed misconduct, two were criminally charged, guards skipped required checks and falsified records, and Epstein was left without a cellmate after an apparent July 23 suicide attempt.
what: Epstein was arrested at Teterboro Airport on 6 July 2019 and indicted in Manhattan for sex trafficking of minors in 2002–2005. Bail was denied on 18 July. He died in his cell on 10 August 2019; the medical examiner ruled suicide by hanging and the case was dismissed on 29 August 2019. The DOJ Inspector General's June 2023 report found no evidence contradicting suicide but documented staff failures that made it possible.

title: Ghislaine Maxwell — convicted of sex trafficking of a minor
who: Ghislaine Maxwell
cover_up: In July 2025 Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche interviewed Maxwell with limited immunity; on 1 Aug 2025 she was moved to the minimum-security Federal Prison Camp Bryan, Texas. A DOJ official recorded secretly said the transfer was against policy (DOJ said he had no role).
what: Maxwell was arrested on 2 July 2020 in Bradford, New Hampshire. On 29 December 2021 a jury convicted her on five of six counts, including sex trafficking of a minor; she was acquitted of enticing a minor to travel. She was sentenced on 28 June 2022 to 20 years. The Second Circuit upheld the conviction on 17 Sept 2024 and the US Supreme Court declined her appeal on 6 Oct 2025; she had argued Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement shielded co-conspirators. As of mid-2026 her lawyer said he would seek a pardon; Blanche said in May 2026 he would not recommend one.

title: Jean-Luc Brunel — Paris investigation into rape of minors (died before trial)
who: Jean-Luc Brunel; MC2 Model Management (New York/Miami), Karin Models
what: Paris prosecutors opened an inquiry in August 2019 into sex trafficking and sexual-assault allegations linked to Epstein, focused on French victims and French suspects. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel, who co-founded Karin Models in 1977 and later founded MC2 Model Management in the US with funding from Epstein, was detained at Charles de Gaulle airport in December 2020 as he tried to board a flight to Senegal, and was placed under formal investigation on suspicion of rape of minors and trafficking of minors for sexual exploitation. He was found hanged in his cell at La Santé prison on 19 Feb 2022, having been held for over a year. He denied wrongdoing and was never tried.

title: US Virgin Islands government suits — Epstein estate and JPMorgan
who: Epstein estate; JPMorgan Chase; Deutsche Bank
cover_up: Banks were alleged to have facilitated and concealed the operation by keeping Epstein as a client. New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150m in July 2020 for ignoring red flags on Epstein. UK regulators permanently banned former JPMorgan banker Jes Staley (upheld June 2025) for recklessly misleading them about his Epstein relationship.
what: Epstein owned the private island of Little St. James in the US Virgin Islands. The territory's government reached a $105m settlement with Epstein's estate and a $62.5m settlement with billionaire Leon Black. In December 2022 it sued JPMorgan Chase, claiming the bank ignored warning signs and facilitated Epstein's activities; JPMorgan agreed in June 2023 to pay $290m to nearly 200 Epstein victims in a class action and in September 2023 to pay the Virgin Islands $75m. The settlements carried no criminal findings.

title: Zorro Ranch, New Mexico — state probe dropped in 2019, reopened 2026
who: Jeffrey Epstein; New Mexico law enforcement
cover_up: The state AG's 2019 investigation was closed at the request of the US Attorney's Office (SDNY). The 2026 interim commission report found Epstein likely got 'preferential treatment' from New Mexico law enforcement, avoided sex-offender registration via a loophole, and used NDAs, secrecy protocols and a $7m-a-year payroll to keep activity out of view. The FBI never searched the ranch in 2019.
what: Epstein bought the 7,600-acre ranch in 1993. New Mexico AG Raúl Torrez reopened a criminal investigation on 12 March 2026 citing previously sealed FBI files, and state officials searched the ranch in March 2026 with the new owners' cooperation. A four-member legislative truth commission created in the 2026 session released a 119-page interim report on 5 Aug 2026; a final report is due by end of 2026. Allegations that bodies were buried near the ranch, raised in the files, are unconfirmed.

title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor — civil settlement, loss of titles, 2026 arrest (misconduct in public office)
who: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor (formerly Prince Andrew, Duke of York)
cover_up: Settled civil case with no admission of liability (Feb 2022). In Oct 2025 it was alleged he asked a protection officer to investigate his accuser; the Metropolitan Police took no further action.
what: Virginia Giuffre's court filings from 2014 alleged Epstein trafficked her to Andrew as a minor; he denies it. She sued in New York in Aug 2021; the case settled in Feb 2022 without admission (reported as about £12m). In Oct–Nov 2025 King Charles removed his remaining titles, including 'prince' (letters patent, Nov 2025). On 19 Feb 2026 Thames Valley Police arrested him on suspicion of misconduct in public office over reports from the DOJ files that he sent confidential trade-envoy reports to Epstein in 2010; he was released under investigation the same day. No sexual-offence charge exists; he denies wrongdoing; the investigation is ongoing.

title: Peter Mandelson — 2026 arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office (Epstein files)
who: Peter Mandelson (former UK ambassador to the US, former cabinet minister)
what: Mandelson was dismissed as UK ambassador to the US in Sept 2025 after emails showed he kept up his friendship with Epstein after Epstein's 2008 conviction. After the January 2026 DOJ release suggested he passed sensitive government information to Epstein about 15 years earlier, he left the Labour Party and House of Lords and the Metropolitan Police arrested him on 23 Feb 2026 on suspicion of misconduct in public office. He faces no allegation of sexual misconduct; recorded here for the network's political reach, not as an abuse case.

title: Thorbjørn Jagland — charged with aggravated corruption over Epstein ties
who: Thorbjørn Jagland (former Norwegian PM, Council of Europe Secretary General, Nobel Committee chair)
what: After the US Justice Department's 2026 release of Epstein documents, Norway's economic-crime agency Økokrim opened an investigation into former prime minister and Council of Europe secretary-general Thorbjørn Jagland on suspicion of aggravated corruption, looking into 'whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position'. On 12 Feb 2026 his lawyers said he had been charged with aggravated corruption; his Oslo home and two other properties were searched. He denies all charges. This is a corruption case, not an abuse charge; recorded for the network's political reach.

title: Ankara prosecutors' inquiry into alleged trafficking of girls from Turkey to Epstein
who: Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor's Office (inquiry)
what: On 23 Dec 2025 Ankara prosecutors reportedly opened an inquiry after opposition MP Turhan Çömez cited the DOJ files. The underlying document is a May 2009 civil complaint by 'Jane Doe No. 102' alleging 'upon information and belief' that Epstein brought minor girls from 'Turkey, the Czech Republic, Asia, and numerous other countries'. Prosecutors are reviewing the files; no findings or charges have been reported.

title: Epstein Files Transparency Act and DOJ releases (2025–2026)
who: US Department of Justice; FBI; House Oversight Committee
cover_up: DOJ said it identified about 6 million potentially responsive pages but released about 3.5 million, withholding about 200,000 under privilege, abuse material and victim-identity grounds; critics in both parties said it broke the law. Faulty redactions exposed at least 43 victims' names (WSJ). The DOJ Inspector General opened a compliance review in April 2026.
what: A 7 July 2025 DOJ/FBI memo said there was no incriminating 'client list', no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent people, and that his death was suicide; it also said Epstein 'harmed over one thousand victims'. Congress then passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act 427–1 in the House and by unanimous consent in the Senate, and it was signed on 19 Nov 2025. DOJ began releasing files on 19 Dec 2025 and on 30 Jan 2026 published over 3 million more pages (about 3.5 million in total), saying notable individuals were not redacted and warning that the release may include fake or false material submitted by the public. On 5 Mar 2026, after an NPR investigation found pages had been withheld, DOJ published 16 more pages. The releases documented Epstein's continued contact with prominent people after 2008 and led to police inquiries and resignations abroad; they did not establish a

title: Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services
who: Claims about US and Israeli intelligence (unproven)
what: In July 2019 journalist Vicky Ward (Daily Beast) reported that Alexander Acosta had told Trump transition interviewers he was told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone; the source was not named. In its November 2020 report, the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility said Acosta told it 'the answer is no' when asked whether Epstein was an intelligence asset, and found 'no evidence suggesting that Epstein was such a cooperating witness or intelligence asset'. Other claims circulate, including that Ghislaine Maxwell's father Robert Maxwell worked for Israeli intelligence and about Epstein's business ties to former Israeli PM Ehud Barak, who denies wrongdoing. No official body has found that Epstein worked for any intelligence service.

title: Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC)
who: Jimmy Savile (BBC broadcaster); BBC; NHS hospitals; Metropolitan Police
network: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
cover_up: Earliest known police report dates from 1958, with police intelligence from 1963; Surrey Police investigated in 2007–09 without charges. A BBC Newsnight investigation was shelved in December 2011; the Pollard Review called the decision flawed.
what: After Savile's death in October 2011, an ITV documentary, 'Exposure: The Other Side of Jimmy Savile', broadcast on 3 Oct 2012, carried accounts of abuse of under-age teenage girls. The Metropolitan Police opened a criminal investigation, Operation Yewtree, on 19 Oct 2012. The January 2013 Met/NSPCC report 'Giving Victims a Voice' recorded 214 crimes across 28 police force areas, including 34 rape or penetration offences, from 1955 to 2009; 450 people had made allegations against him, 73% of them under 18 at the time. The CPS apologised for missing the chance to prosecute him in 2009. The report found no clear evidence that he operated in a paedophile ring.

title: Dame Janet Smith Review — Savile and Stuart Hall at the BBC
who: BBC
network: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
cover_up: Some BBC staff knew of complaints about Savile and Hall but did not pass them to senior management; Hall's celebrity status discouraged staff from escalating.
what: The independent review by Dame Janet Smith, published on 25 February 2016, found that Savile sexually abused 72 people in connection with his BBC work, raping eight, the youngest victim aged eight; incidents dated back to 1959. It found that Stuart Hall assaulted 21 girls and women in connection with the BBC between 1967 and 1991, the youngest aged 10. Some staff knew of complaints, but a 'culture of fear' and deference to stars meant these were not passed to senior managers; two senior managers were 'aware' or 'probably aware' of Hall's assaults on BBC premises.

title: Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals
who: NHS hospitals (Leeds General Infirmary, Stoke Mandeville, Broadmoor and others)
network: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
what: Kate Lampard's lessons-learned report (26 February 2015) drew on 44 NHS investigation reports — 28 published in June 2014 and 16 more alongside her report — and found Savile's known victims in NHS hospitals were aged five to 75, including patients, staff and visitors; his status gave him keys and virtually unfettered access to wards. At Leeds General Infirmary 64 people came forward and 60 alleged abuse on the premises, between 1962 and 2009, including three rapes.

title: Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale
who: Cyril Smith (Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992); Lancashire Constabulary; Director of Public Prosecutions; Rochdale Council
cover_up: Police evidence presented in 1970 led to no action; the CPS said in 2012 that Smith should have been charged and that he had been given an assurance in 1970 he would not be prosecuted. Press allegations in 1979 (Rochdale Alternative Press, Private Eye) produced no prosecution. He was knighted in 1988 though Margaret Thatcher had been told of the allegations.
what: Cyril Smith, Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992, was alleged by eight men to have indecently assaulted them as teenagers in about 1961–1966; six had lived at Cambridge House hostel, which he helped set up. The Director of Public Prosecutions advised against prosecution in 1970, and CPS reviews in 1998 and 1999 did not lead to charges. He died on 3 September 2010, never charged. On 27 November 2012 Greater Manchester Police said the boys had been victims of physical and sexual abuse by Smith, and the CPS said he should have been charged. The IICSA report on Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale (April 2018) found no evidence of improper influence on the DPP but said valuable opportunities to prosecute were lost in 1998 and 1999, and that discussions before his 1988 knighthood showed 'considerable deference to power'; witnesses also told it Smith assaulted boys at Knowl View School.

title: Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims
who: Elm Guest House; Metropolitan Police (Operation Fernbridge)
what: Police placed the guest house near Barnes Common under surveillance from late 1981 after concerns about a 10-year-old boy there, raided it on 19 June 1982 and arrested 20 people; the owners were convicted of running a disorderly house. Claims spread in later decades that politicians and other prominent people attended abuse parties there. Giving evidence to IICSA on 7 March 2019, Met Commander Neil Jerome said police had found evidence of abuse of only one child, the 10-year-old boy, whose account and a medical examination showed he had been extensively abused; no prominent or well-known person was seen during surveillance or found in the raid; an IOPC investigation found 'no substance' in the claim that the boy named an 'Uncle Leon'; and the online 'Elm Guest House list' had 'zero evidential value'. The abuse of the boy occurred; the VIP claims are unsupported.

title: Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims
who: Metropolitan Police; Carl Beech (complainant)
what: Between November 2014 and March 2016 the Met investigated Carl Beech's claims that a VIP ring of politicians and military and security chiefs abused boys and committed murders, including at Dolphin Square. It searched homes of named suspects, including Leon Brittan, Harvey Proctor and Lord Bramall, but arrested and charged no one. Sir Richard Henriques's review (Nov 2016) found police had been taken in by false allegations and listed 43 failings. In July 2019 Beech was jailed for 18 years for 12 counts of perverting the course of justice and one of fraud, and for child sexual offences he had admitted, including possessing indecent images of children and covertly filming a teenage boy.

title: IICSA Westminster report — deference and failures (no proven 'VIP ring')
who: Parliament; political parties; police; Director of Public Prosecutions
cover_up: Example of documented deference: in 1978 diplomat Peter Hayman left child-abuse-related material on a London bus; police found 45 diaries of sexual fantasies about children, but the DPP advised no prosecution; Attorney General Havers defended this in 1981 after MP Geoffrey Dickens named Hayman in the Commons.
what: IICSA held an investigation into allegations of child sexual abuse linked to Westminster (report February 2020). Its findings are NOT summarised here because the report could not be opened in this pass; check before publishing. What is documented from opened sources: the Hayman case (no prosecution in 1978–81 despite seized material) and IICSA evidence on Elm Guest House (see that record).

title: Rolf Harris — convicted of indecent assault of girls
who: Rolf Harris (entertainer)
what: Arrested in March 2013 under Operation Yewtree, Harris was found guilty on 30 June 2014 of 12 counts of indecent assault against four girls and young women between 1968 and 1986. He was sentenced to five years nine months. In November 2017 the Court of Appeal quashed one conviction (the alleged assault of an eight-year-old in Portsmouth in 1969) and upheld the other 11. He died on 10 May 2023.

title: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
what: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing thousands of child abuse images (about 4,000; jailed four months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002 amid sex-crime allegations. In March 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11; he spent about two and a half years in jail there. In February 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape, four indecent assaults and one count of sex with a girl under 13, against three girls in 1975–1980, and sentenced to 16 years. Released in February 2023, he was recalled to prison in March 2023 for breaching licence conditions.

title: Stuart Hall — indecent assault of girls (BBC presenter)
who: Stuart Hall (BBC broadcaster)
network: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
what: In May 2013 Hall pleaded guilty to 14 counts of indecent assault on 13 girls aged 9 to 17 between 1967 and 1986; his 15-month sentence was doubled to 30 months by the Court of Appeal as unduly lenient. In May 2014 he admitted one further indecent assault on a 13-year-old girl and was found guilty of another against the same girl, receiving an extra two years six months (five years in total). He was cleared of rape charges.

title: Max Clifford — indecent assault
who: Max Clifford (publicist)
what: Clifford was convicted in April 2014 of eight counts of indecent assault against four women and girls, the youngest 15, between 1977 and 1984, and jailed for eight years. His challenge to the sentence failed in November 2014. He died in prison custody in December 2017; the Court of Appeal upheld his convictions posthumously in April 2019.

title: Operation Yewtree — post-Savile investigation of public figures
who: Metropolitan Police
what: Launched by the Metropolitan Police on 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations, Yewtree had arrested 19 people by October 2015. Those convicted include Paul Gadd (Gary Glitter), Max Clifford, Rolf Harris, former DJ Chris Denning, Dave Lee Travis (one count, involving an adult) and, in April 2017, ex-BBC worker Geoffrey Wheeler, which the BBC called the operation's sixth conviction; Stoke Mandeville doctor Michael Salmon was also convicted in 2015 after a Yewtree investigation. Others were acquitted or never charged, including several well-known names, and must not be described as offenders.

title: Huw Edwards — indecent images of children
who: Huw Edwards (BBC newsreader)
cover_up: The BBC kept paying him after his November 2023 arrest; it later asked him to repay over £200,000.
what: BBC newsreader Huw Edwards was arrested in November 2023 and pleaded guilty on 31 July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children, received via WhatsApp from another man between December 2020 and August 2021 (41 of 377 sexual images sent were indecent images of children). On 16 Sept 2024 he received six months suspended for two years.

title: Barry Bennell and English youth football (Sheldon Review)
who: Barry Bennell (coach/scout, Crewe Alexandra, Manchester City links); The Football Association
cover_up: Crewe Alexandra heard an allegation but kept Bennell on with restrictions (former director Hamilton Smith). The Sheldon Review found the FA guilty of 'institutional failure' for delaying safeguards after 1995.
what: Bennell was first jailed in Florida in 1994 for raping a British boy on a football tour, then received prison sentences in Britain in 1998, 2015, February 2018 (50 offences against 12 boys aged eight to 14, 1979–1990; 30 years) and October 2020 (a fifth sentence, making 34 years in total). After a former player spoke out publicly in November 2016, BBC News reported within weeks that 350 people had alleged they were victims, linked to 55 clubs. Clive Sheldon QC's review for the FA (17 Mar 2021) recorded at least 240 suspects and 692 survivors across football, said the true numbers were likely far higher, found the FA had acted 'far too slowly' on child protection, and criticised Manchester City, Crewe and Stoke over Bennell. Bennell died in prison in September 2023.

title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — elite boarding schools (Fettes, Loretto, Gordonstoun, Edinburgh Academy, Merchiston)
who: Fettes College, Loretto School, Gordonstoun, Edinburgh Academy, Merchiston Castle School
cover_up: Fettes dismissed teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial; he went on to teach in South Africa.
what: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry, launched in 2015 and led by Lady Smith, has heard evidence of abuse at elite independent schools including Edinburgh Academy, Fettes College, Gordonstoun, Loretto and Merchiston; Gordonstoun has apologised to anyone abused in its care. Former teacher Iain Wares, accused by scores of former pupils of Edinburgh Academy and Fettes, where he taught in the 1960s and 1970s, admitted in South African extradition documents that he had touched students inappropriately at Edinburgh Academy. South Africa approved the UK's extradition request in 2020 and the Cape Town High Court ruled in 2024 that he could be extradited on three charges; in October 2025 he was arrested in South Africa on a further 90 charges. He has not been tried.

title: Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures
who: Marc Dutroux, Michelle Martin, Michel Lelièvre; Belgian Gendarmerie and judicial police
cover_up: Dutroux was released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence over prosecutor and psychiatrist objections. Police missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and unreviewed videotapes; rivalry between Gendarmerie and judicial police hampered the hunt. Judge Connerotte was removed in Oct 1996 for attending a victims' fundraising dinner.
what: Dutroux, on parole for earlier rapes, kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19 in 1995–96; he was found guilty of kidnapping and raping all six, killing two and causing the deaths of two others. He was arrested in August 1996, and in October 1996 hundreds of thousands of Belgians joined the White March in Brussels to protest police and judicial failures. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by Marc Verwilghen sharply criticised the police investigation. On 22 June 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life; his ex-wife Michelle Martin got 30 years and Michel Lelièvre 25; businessman Michel Nihoul was acquitted of kidnapping and conspiracy but convicted of drug trafficking and other crimes (five years). Belgium later reorganised its police forces.

title: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network
who: Witnesses X1–X4 (claims); Belgian prosecutors
what: Witnesses told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Marc Dutroux, Michel Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed the statements, and investigators were criticised for leading a key witness; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. In 1999 the Guardian reported renewed cover-up claims, and that the parliamentary inquiry's chair said his findings had been muzzled. The claims of an elite network remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.

title: Casa Pia — abuse of children in state care by a TV presenter, diplomat and others
who: Casa Pia (state children's institution); Carlos Cruz (TV presenter); Jorge Ritto (ex-ambassador); Hugo Marçal (lawyer); Ferreira Diniz (doctor); Manuel Abrantes (Casa Pia official); Carlos Silvino (driver)
cover_up: A teacher reportedly began reporting abuse to Casa Pia leaders and police in 1975, and police accused a caretaker in 1981, without legal action. Ritto had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969–71 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but stayed in the diplomatic service.
what: Abuse at Casa Pia, a state institution caring for about 4,500 children, is said to have begun in the mid-1970s and came to light in 2002. After a trial that began in 2004, on 3 Sept 2010 six of seven defendants were convicted: former Casa Pia driver Carlos Silvino (18 years, after confessing to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others), TV presenter Carlos Cruz (7), doctor João Ferreira Diniz (7), retired ambassador Jorge Ritto (6y8m), lawyer Hugo Marçal (6y2m) and former Casa Pia governor Manuel Abrantes (5y9m); a woman accused of letting her house be used was acquitted. The convicted men other than Silvino denied the charges. Former minister Paulo Pedroso was detained during the investigation but was not tried.

title: Joris Demmink allegations (Netherlands) — investigated, never charged
who: Allegations against the former Secretary-General of the Dutch Ministry of Justice
what: In 2007 a Turkish man serving a life sentence alleged that Joris Demmink, then the top civil servant at the Dutch justice ministry, raped two boys aged 12 and 14 in Turkey in the late 1990s; a lawyer filed a criminal complaint for one of them in 2010. After an initial inquiry found no evidence, an appeals court ordered a formal criminal investigation. Turkey repeatedly refused requests to hear witnesses, and the examining judge closed the inquiry in May 2016. In August 2017 prosecutors dropped the case, saying checks of his papers, bank and travel records found no evidence he was in Turkey at the time and that a Turkish document claiming he was there was fake. Demmink was never charged and denies the allegations.

title: Gabriel Matzneff — writer's published accounts of abusing minors
who: Gabriel Matzneff (author); French literary establishment (Gallimard and others)
cover_up: Literary tolerance: Matzneff published diaries describing sex with minors and child sex tourism in the Philippines (e.g. 1985) and was celebrated on TV (Apostrophes, 1990).
what: From the 1960s Matzneff wrote openly about sex with adolescents and was feted by the Paris literary world. In the memoir 'Le Consentement' (published January 2020) its author, a publishing executive, described their relationship when she was 14. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation for rape of a minor in January 2020, and Gallimard withdrew his journals from sale. The BBC noted that, given the time elapsed, the case was unlikely to lead to charges. In November 2023 prosecutors opened a second investigation after another woman accused him of raping her as a child. He has not been convicted.

title: Olivier Duhamel — incest allegation ('La Familia grande')
who: Olivier Duhamel (constitutional scholar, head of Sciences Po foundation FNSP)
what: In January 2021 his stepdaughter's book 'La Familia grande' alleged that Duhamel had sexually abused her twin brother, his stepson, as a young teenager over two or three years in the late 1980s. Duhamel resigned from his posts, including the Sciences Po foundation, and Paris prosecutors opened an investigation. In April 2021 French media, citing sources close to the inquiry, reported that he admitted the abuse when questioned by police. He cannot be prosecuted because the statute of limitations has lapsed.

title: Joël Le Scouarnec — surgeon convicted for 299 victims
who: Joël Le Scouarnec (surgeon); hospitals and medical regulators
cover_up: The FBI traced his downloading of abuse images in 2004; his 2005 conviction (4 months suspended) brought no restriction on practice. Prosecutors did not alert medical authorities; the regional medical body found no breach in 2006; a 2007 warning to the health ministry brought no action; a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction.
what: Le Scouarnec, a surgeon in western France, was convicted in Saintes in December 2020 of raping and sexually assaulting four children, including two of his nieces (15 years). At his second trial in Vannes he admitted abusing all 299 victims, mostly hospital patients, many under anaesthesia or waking from surgery, between 1989 and 2014; more than 250 were under 15. On 28 May 2025 the court sentenced him to the maximum 20 years. He is not part of an elite network; included as a professional whose standing protected him (setting is debatable — could be moved to 'care').

title: Hungary — presidential pardon in Bicske children's-home cover-up case
who: President Katalin Novák; Justice Minister Judit Varga; Bicske children's home
cover_up: In April 2023 the president pardoned the home's former deputy director, Endre Kónya, who had been convicted of helping cover up the director's sexual abuse of children.
what: In April 2023, ahead of a papal visit, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, among them the former deputy director of the Bicske children's home, who had been sentenced in 2022 to three years four months for helping the home's director cover up his sexual abuse of children. The pardon became public in early February 2024 (reported by Telex on 2 Feb). After protests, Novák resigned on 10 Feb 2024, saying she had made a mistake; former justice minister Judit Varga, who countersigned the pardon, announced the same day that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Orbán proposed a constitutional amendment barring pardons for crimes against children.

title: Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire children's homes; never tried
who: Greville Janner (Labour MP and peer); Leicestershire Police; Crown Prosecution Service
cover_up: Police investigated in 1991, 2002 and 2007 without charges. The Henriques report (Jan 2016) found the CPS and police at fault and said a prosecution was likely to have succeeded in 1991, 2002 or 2007. A 2021 review found police 'appeared reluctant to fully investigate'.
what: Allegations that Janner abused boys in Leicestershire children's homes first emerged publicly in 1991. In April 2015 the CPS decided not to charge him because of dementia; an independent review reversed this in June 2015, but he was found unfit to stand trial in Dec 2015 and died on 19 Dec 2015 before a 'trial of the facts'. He was never convicted. A January 2016 report by retired judge Sir Richard Henriques found that the CPS and Leicestershire Police had mishandled investigations in 1991, 2002 and 2007 and that there had been enough evidence to prosecute him in 2007.

title: Lord Nazir Ahmed — convicted of offences against two children in the 1970s
who: Nazir Ahmed (former Labour peer)
what: On 5 Jan 2022 Sheffield Crown Court convicted the former peer of two counts of attempted rape of a girl and a serious sexual assault on a boy, committed in Rotherham in 1971–1974 when he was a teenager. He was sentenced to 5½ years, reduced to 2½ years on appeal in March 2023 because he was a child at the time. He had resigned from the Lords in November 2020 before an expulsion recommended over a separate complaint was carried out.

title: Imran Ahmad Khan MP — sexual assault of a 15-year-old boy
who: Imran Ahmad Khan (Conservative MP for Wakefield)
what: A sitting MP, Khan was convicted on 11 Apr 2022 of sexually assaulting a 15-year-old boy in 2008, expelled from the Conservative Party, resigned his seat, and was sentenced to 18 months; his appeal failed in Dec 2022.

title: Sebastian Edathy (Bundestag) — images of naked minors; case closed on payment
who: Sebastian Edathy (SPD member of the Bundestag)
cover_up: Interior Minister Hans-Peter Friedrich resigned on 14 Feb 2014 after being accused of disclosing the investigation to SPD leaders.
what: Edathy gave up his Bundestag seat in February 2014, and his homes and offices were then searched; Hanover prosecutors said he had placed nine orders for 31 products with a company in Canada. On 2 March 2015, at his trial before the Verden regional court, his lawyer admitted on his behalf that he had downloaded videos and images of naked boys using his official laptop, and the court ended the case against a €5,000 payment to the children's charity Kinderschutzbund; he has no criminal record from it, and he said afterwards that his statement was not a confession.

title: Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring
who: Jean Succar Kuri (hotelier); associates named in Lydia Cacho's reporting
cover_up: See the related record on journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 arrest arranged after her book exposed the ring.
what: Cancún hotel businessman Succar Kuri was detained in the United States (reported as Los Angeles/Arizona) in 2004 at the request of Mexico's federal prosecutors and Interpol, after complaints by several girls, and was later returned to Mexico. In 2011 a federal district court convicted him and sentenced him to 13 years; on appeal by both sides a Cancún appeals court raised the sentence to 112 years, which was upheld. In 2023 a federal circuit court annulled the 112-year sentence over procedural flaws and ordered a new ruling on sexual abuse and child pornography offences against seven minors, which reduced his term. He died in Cancún on 14 June 2024 while still serving his sentence. Journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' described him as the head of a child-exploitation network and linked him to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Governor Mario Marín.

title: Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring
who: Mario Marín (Governor of Puebla); Kamel Nacif Borge (businessman)
cover_up: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.
what: After journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' (2005) linked Cancún businessman Jean Succar Kuri's child-exploitation network to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Puebla governor Mario Marín, Cacho was arrested in 2005 and says she was tortured. Arrest warrants for torture were issued against Marín and Nacif; Marín was arrested in Acapulco in February 2021, and Nacif was detained in Lebanon in May 2021 and later released there. Marín was moved to house arrest in August 2024, returned to prison in April 2025, and in July 2026 was again granted house arrest on health and age grounds while his trial for alleged torture of Cacho continues. Neither has been convicted; both are accused of torture, not of the abuse itself.

title: Spiniak case, Chile — child exploitation ring and false accusation against a senator
who: Claudio Spiniak (businessman)
what: Businessman Claudio Spiniak was arrested in 2003 accused of leading a network that sexually abused and exploited adolescents. In 2008 Chile's Supreme Court sentenced him to 12 years for sexual abuse of minors, promoting their exploitation and producing pornographic material; he was released in 2013 and died in March 2026. A witness claimed that members of Congress attended his parties — claims publicly backed by a deputy and a former priest — but she later admitted she had lied; the politicians named were cleared (proceedings dismissed for lack of evidence). The political-network claim is disproved.

title: Larry Nassar — USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University
who: Larry Nassar (team doctor); USA Gymnastics; Michigan State University; FBI; US Olympic & Paralympic Committee
cover_up: Athletes complained as early as 1997. USAG was told on 17 June 2015. The DOJ Inspector General (July 2021) found FBI agents failed to act on the gymnasts' reports and that supervisory agent W. Jay Abbott later lied about it. MSU dean William Strampel was convicted of misconduct in office (2019); charges against ex-MSU president Lou Anna Simon (dismissed 2020) and ex-USAG CEO Steve Penny (dropped 2
what: Nassar pleaded guilty to federal child-abuse-image charges (60 years, Dec 2017) and to criminal sexual conduct in two Michigan counties, receiving 40–175 years in Ingham County (Jan 2018) and 40–125 years in Eaton County (Feb 2018); by the final hearing the number of identified victims had reached 265. Settlements: Michigan State University $500m to more than 300 women and girls (2018); USA Gymnastics and the USOPC $380m (2021); the US government $138.7m to 139 claimants over FBI failures to investigate promptly (April 2024). The Indianapolis Star's September 2016 investigation triggered the case.

title: Jerry Sandusky — Penn State football and The Second Mile
who: Jerry Sandusky (assistant coach); Pennsylvania State University; The Second Mile charity
cover_up: A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted. In 2001 graduate assistant Mike McQueary reported seeing Sandusky with a boy in a shower; it went to Joe Paterno, athletic director Tim Curley and vice-president Gary Schultz. The Freeh report (July 2012) found Paterno, president Graham Spanier, Curley and Schultz concealed Sandusky's activities. Curley, Schultz and Spanier were convicted of c
what: Sandusky, a former Penn State assistant football coach, was charged in Nov 2011 and convicted in June 2012 of 45 counts of sexual abuse involving 10 boys, some assaulted on the Penn State campus; in Oct 2012 he was sentenced to 30–60 years. He met boys through The Second Mile charity he founded in 1977. The Freeh report (July 2012), commissioned by the university, found the most senior Penn State leaders showed 'total disregard' for the victims' safety. The NCAA fined Penn State $60m.

title: Dennis Hastert — former House Speaker admitted abusing boys he coached
who: Dennis Hastert (Speaker of the US House 1999–2007; former wrestling coach)
cover_up: Hush money: he withdrew about $952,000 in structured cash payments to a former student; the statute of limitations meant no sex-crime charge was possible.
what: Hastert was indicted in May 2015 for structuring cash withdrawals and lying to the FBI, and in October 2015 pleaded guilty to one count of structuring about $950,000 in withdrawals made to pay a former student to hide past wrongdoing. Prosecutors said in April 2016 that he had sexually abused at least four boys when he was a wrestling coach at Yorkville High School (1965–1981). At sentencing on 27 April 2016 he admitted abusing boys he coached; the judge called him a 'serial child molester' and sentenced him to 15 months. He was never convicted of a sexual offence, because the statute of limitations had expired.

title: Mark Foley — messages to congressional pages; House leadership 'negligent'
who: Rep. Mark Foley; House Republican leadership
cover_up: Complaints reached House staff and leaders around 2000–2005. The House Ethics Committee (Dec 2006) found Speaker Hastert and other leaders 'negligent' but recommended no sanctions. Florida's FDLE closed its probe in 2008 citing insufficient evidence and said Congress and Foley denied it access to data.
what: In late September 2006 sexually suggestive emails and instant messages from Rep. Mark Foley to teenage boys who had served as House pages became public; he resigned on 29 Sept 2006. On 8 Dec 2006 the House Ethics Committee found Republican members and staff had been negligent in handling earlier warnings about his conduct but that no House rules were broken, and recommended no punishment. No criminal charges were brought; Florida's state investigation was closed in September 2008 citing insufficient evidence.

title: Joel Greenberg conviction and House Ethics findings on Matt Gaetz
who: Joel Greenberg (Seminole County tax collector); Rep. Matt Gaetz (not charged)
what: Greenberg pleaded guilty in May 2021 to six federal crimes, including sex trafficking of a minor (a 17-year-old girl in 2017), identity theft, stalking, wire fraud and conspiracy to bribe a public official, and was sentenced to 11 years on 1 Dec 2022. DOJ investigated Rep. Gaetz over whether he paid the same 17-year-old for sex but did not charge him. The House Ethics Committee report (23 Dec 2024) said it received testimony that Gaetz twice had sex with the 17-year-old at a 2017 party and paid her, and found that this violated Florida law, but found insufficient evidence that he violated the federal sex-trafficking statute. Gaetz denies having sex with a minor and has not been charged.

title: R. Kelly — racketeering and child sexual abuse material convictions
who: Robert Kelly (singer) and his entourage (racketeering enterprise)
cover_up: He was acquitted in 2008 of child pornography charges brought in 2002, despite Chicago Sun-Times reporting from 2000.
what: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Kelly on 27 Sept 2021 of racketeering, including acts of bribery and sexual exploitation of a child, and of Mann Act sex-trafficking offences; he was sentenced to 30 years. In September 2022 a Chicago federal jury convicted him of three counts of producing child sexual abuse material and three of enticing a minor; in February 2023 he was sentenced to 20 years, 19 of them to run concurrently with the New York term. The 2019 documentary 'Surviving R. Kelly' led to the new prosecutions.

title: Jared Fogle (Subway spokesman) — child abuse material and paid sex with minors
who: Jared Fogle; Russell Taylor (co-conspirator); Subway
cover_up: Allegations surfaced in 2007 but the FBI acted only in 2015. A franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 about Fogle's messages seeking sex with a minor; Subway says it has no record.
what: After his Indianapolis home was raided in July 2015 in a child abuse material investigation, Fogle pleaded guilty to receiving child abuse material and travelling to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor, and on 19 Nov 2015 was sentenced to 188 months (15 years 8 months). He had already paid $100,000 restitution to each of 14 victims ($1.4m); two were 16 and 17 when he travelled to have sex with them.

title: Brian Peck — Nickelodeon dialogue coach convicted of abusing a child actor
who: Brian Peck (Nickelodeon dialogue coach)
cover_up: Several entertainment-industry figures wrote letters supporting Peck at sentencing in 2004; some apologised in 2024.
what: Peck, a dialogue coach on Nickelodeon shows, was arrested by the LAPD on 19 Aug 2003 on 11 charges. He pleaded no contest to two: a lewd act upon a child aged 14 or 15 by a person 10 years older, and oral copulation of a person under 16; the court found him guilty on both and in October 2004 sentenced him to 16 months, and he was required to register as a sex offender. The victim, then a child actor on a Nickelodeon show, identified himself publicly in the March 2024 documentary 'Quiet on Set'.

title: Roman Polanski — 1977 guilty plea, fugitive since 1978
who: Roman Polanski (film director)
cover_up: Fled to France on 1 Feb 1978 before sentencing; Switzerland (2010) and Poland (2015–16) refused US extradition.
what: Arrested in 1977 and charged with a string of offences involving a 13-year-old girl, Polanski pleaded guilty to unlawful sexual intercourse with a minor in a plea bargain. He fled to the UK and then France in 1978, before sentencing, and has lived mainly in France since. Swiss police detained him in September 2009 and held him under house arrest, but Switzerland refused the US extradition request in 2010. A Polish court refused extradition in October 2015 and Poland's Supreme Court upheld that refusal on 6 Dec 2016. A civil suit alleging he raped an underage girl in 1973 was settled in 2024 before trial; he denies that allegation.

title: Michael Jackson — 1993 allegations settled, 2005 acquittal
who: Michael Jackson (singer)
what: A 1993 allegation by a 13-year-old boy led to an out-of-court civil settlement for an undisclosed amount; Jackson was not charged in that case and denied wrongdoing. After a 2003 complaint by another boy, he was charged in December 2003 and indicted by a grand jury in April 2004 on 10 counts, including lewd conduct with a child under 14, administering alcohol and conspiracy. A jury acquitted him on all counts on 13 June 2005. No criminal finding exists against him; he died in 2009.

title: Graham James — junior hockey coach (Western Hockey League)
who: Graham James (coach/GM, Swift Current Broncos, Calgary Hitmen)
cover_up: He received a federal pardon in 2007, which became public in 2010.
what: James was convicted in 1997 of sexually assaulting three junior players he coached, and sentenced to 3½ years. After a former player's 2009 memoir and police complaint, he pleaded guilty in Dec 2011 to molesting two more players when they were teenagers; the two-year sentence was raised to five years by the Manitoba Court of Appeal in Feb 2013.

title: USA Swimming — coaches banned for abuse; claims mishandled
who: USA Swimming
what: USA Swimming banned prominent coach Rick Curl for life in September 2012; a former swimmer said he had abused her from age 12 in 1983–1986. A February 2018 Orange County Register investigation reported that hundreds of swimmers were sexually abused over decades and that people in charge knew and ignored it, and that USA Swimming had banned 138 coaches and officials for life for sexual abuse and misconduct. Former coach Andy King, reported to Pacific Swimming officials in 2003, was arrested in 2009 and sentenced to 40 years after pleading no contest to 20 counts of felony child molestation, some victims as young as 10.

title: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska
who: Claims against Lawrence E. King Jr. (Franklin Community Federal Credit Union) and prominent Nebraskans
what: After the Franklin Community Federal Credit Union in Omaha failed in late 1988 and its manager Lawrence King was accused of embezzling millions, rumours spread that its money had paid for the sexual abuse of minors by prominent Nebraskans. In July 1990 a Douglas County grand jury called the claims a 'carefully crafted hoax' and indicted two people for perjury; a federal grand jury in September 1990 also found the allegations unfounded. King called the sexual allegations 'garbage'. A later civil default judgment against King, who did not respond, is not a finding of fact.

title: 'Pizzagate' — false claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria
who: Online conspiracy theory targeting Democratic politicians
what: In Oct–Nov 2016 online posts, citing leaked Podesta emails, falsely claimed that the Comet Ping Pong pizzeria in Washington was home to a child sex-abuse ring involving top Democrats. No victims or evidence emerged. On 4 Dec 2016 Edgar Maddison Welch fired an AR-15 rifle inside to 'investigate'; he pleaded guilty in March 2017 to federal assault with a dangerous weapon and transporting a firearm across state lines, and was sentenced to four years in June 2017.

title: McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals
who: McMartin Preschool (accused: Ray Buckey, Peggy McMartin Buckey)
what: Claims of abuse at the McMartin Pre-School in Manhattan Beach, California, began in autumn 1983 with one small boy's report and grew to include allegations of 'satanic-like ritual'; interview techniques were later widely criticised. In January 1990, after nearly three years of trial, Peggy McMartin Buckey was acquitted of all 12 counts and Ray Buckey of 40 counts, with the jury deadlocked on 13; a retrial of Ray Buckey on eight counts ended in a deadlocked jury in July 1990, and the prosecution was dropped. None of the seven people charged was convicted of anything. The case cost taxpayers about $14m. Included as the template for 'ritual abuse' claims.

title: Johnny Kitagawa — Johnny & Associates talent agency
who: Johnny Kitagawa (founder, Johnny & Associates; now Smile-Up)
cover_up: Media silence: Shukan Bunshun's 2001 reports were upheld on the sexual allegations by the courts (damages reduced 2003; Supreme Court rejected appeal 2004), yet Japanese media barely covered them; journalists attributed this to the agency's power over talent bookings. Earliest cited report: Weekly Sankei, 1965.
what: An external investigation set up by Johnny & Associates concluded on 29 Aug 2023 that founder Johnny Kitagawa had sexually abused minors aspiring to be pop singers for decades; the BBC summarises the finding as abuse of hundreds of boys and young men over a six-decade career. The company admitted the abuse in September 2023, split into a new talent agency (Starto Entertainment) and Smile-Up, which handles compensation through a relief committee of three former judges. The BBC documentary 'Predator' (March 2023) and a former trainee's public allegations in April 2023 triggered the reckoning. In March 2024 Smile-Up's CEO told the BBC he believed two more perpetrators had worked at the agency. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.

title: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
