cover_up: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.
what: Sengar, then a BJP MLA in Uttar Pradesh, was convicted in December 2019 by a special CBI court in Delhi of raping a minor girl in Unnao district in 2017, and sentenced to life imprisonment; the BJP had expelled him. In December 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; on 29 Dec 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order on the CBI's appeal, and in May 2026 it set the suspension aside, directing the High Court to decide his appeal against conviction within three months or pass a fresh order.

title: Kasur child abuse video scandal (Hussain Khanwala)
who: Local gang filming abuse of children; Punjab police; local MPA (alleged)
cover_up: Punjab police and the local PML-N provincial assembly member Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan were alleged to have tried to cover it up; the Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. Police clashed with protesting villagers on 8 Aug 2015.
what: In August 2015 it emerged that in Hussain Khanwala village, Kasur district, a gang had filmed the sexual abuse of at least 280 children and blackmailed their parents by threatening to leak the videos. Police, who had failed to act despite pleas from parents, made dozens of arrests only after clashes between relatives and authorities drew media attention. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court in Lahore sentenced two men to life imprisonment; Arab News reported in February 2018 that 12 other accused men were acquitted. Placed in 'elite' for the alleged political protection; the protection claims were not verified for this record.

title: Knox Grammar School — headmaster failed to report teachers' abuse
who: Knox Grammar School; Uniting Church
cover_up: The Royal Commission (Sept 2016) found headmaster Ian Paterson never reported a student's abuse allegation to police in about 30 years, despite a duty from 1988; he let accused teachers resign and gave some positive references, and withheld information from a police officer.
what: After abuse was reported to police in 2009, five former Knox Grammar teachers were convicted of child sexual offences against students. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse held Case Study 23 on the school in February–March 2015, examining its handling of concerns about teachers between 1970 and 2009, and heard from 12 former students. Its September 2016 report found that former headmaster Ian Paterson (1969–1998) deliberately covered up allegations, placing the school's reputation ahead of student welfare; he had told the commission he did not tell police what he knew about teachers who were later convicted.

title: Geelong Grammar School — Royal Commission case study 32
who: Geelong Grammar School (Anglican)
cover_up: The Royal Commission found the school repeatedly failed to investigate or report credible allegations, particularly under principal John Lewis (1980–94), and 'placed its own interests ahead of those of victims'. A 2007 settlement with victims of a boarding-house assistant was minuted as 'a very satisfactory financial outcome for the school'.
what: The Royal Commission's Case Study 32 heard from 13 former students who said they were abused by staff between 1956 and 1989. Five staff members were convicted of child sex offences against Geelong Grammar students, including a live-in boarding-house assistant who pleaded guilty in April 2005 to 41 counts of gross indecency and indecent acts and was convicted of offences against 40 students between 1985 and 1995 (six and a half years' jail), and a teacher convicted in 2008 over a 2007 offence. The report was published in December 2016.

title: Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling
who: Brisbane Grammar School; St Paul's School; Anglican Diocese of Brisbane (Archbishop Peter Hollingworth)
cover_up: Brisbane Grammar quietly investigated complaints about counsellor Kevin Lynch in the early 1980s; he moved to St Paul's. A 2003 diocesan inquiry found Archbishop Hollingworth in 1993 allowed a known abuser to keep working as a priest.
what: School counsellor Kevin John Lynch, who worked at Brisbane Grammar and then at the Anglican St Paul's School in the 1980s and 1990s, abused students; music teacher Gregory Knight at St Paul's was a convicted paedophile. Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001. An Anglican church inquiry report, tabled in the Queensland parliament on 1 May 2003, found he had acted unfairly in some cases, notably in allowing a known paedophile to continue as a priest; he resigned as Governor-General on 25 May 2003. In November 2015 the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse examined the two schools' handling of the abuse, and Hollingworth apologised to victims.

title: Timothy Omotoso (Jesus Dominion International) — trafficking and rape charges ended in acquittal
who: Timothy Omotoso (Nigerian televangelist) and two co-accused
cover_up: Whistleblower Pamela Mabini was shot dead outside her home on 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict.
what: Omotoso, senior pastor of Jesus Dominion International, was arrested at an airport in 2017 and charged with 32 counts including rape, human trafficking, racketeering and sexual assault; prosecutors alleged that he and two assistants recruited young women from the church, some as young as 14, and arranged travel to have them abused. On 2 April 2025 the Eastern Cape High Court acquitted him and the two co-accused of all charges, the judge finding that the state had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and criticising the prosecution's handling. He was re-arrested on immigration charges on 10 May 2025.

title: T.B. Joshua (SCOAN) — BBC investigation into abuse of disciples
who: T.B. Joshua; Synagogue Church of All Nations (SCOAN)
what: A BBC Africa Eye investigation published on 8 January 2024 reported corroborating testimony from more than 25 former disciples from seven countries that TB Joshua, founder of the Synagogue Church of All Nations in Lagos, had sexually assaulted and raped followers and subjected them to abuse including solitary confinement, with the most recent experiences in 2019. One woman said he first raped her when she was 17 and that she was made to have forced abortions. Joshua died in June 2021. The church did not respond to the BBC's allegations but has called previous claims unsubstantiated. No official finding. Religious figure placed here for celebrity and political influence.

title: Bob Hewitt — tennis coach convicted of raping girls he coached
who: Bob Hewitt (Grand Slam doubles champion, coach)
what: In March 2015 a Johannesburg court convicted former tennis champion Bob Hewitt of two rapes and one sexual assault of girls he coached; one victim testified he raped her in 1982 when she was 12. In May 2015 he was sentenced to an effective six years; South Africa's Supreme Court of Appeal rejected his appeal against sentence in June 2016. The International Tennis Hall of Fame suspended him in 2012 and expelled him in 2016.

title: Haitian Football Federation — Yves Jean-Bart banned by FIFA
who: Yves Jean-Bart (FHF president since 2000)
what: On 30 April 2020 The Guardian reported accusations that Jean-Bart, president of the Haitian Football Federation since 2000, coerced young female players at the national training centre in Croix-des-Bouquets into sex; he denies the allegations. On 18 Nov 2020 FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him from football for life. On 14 Feb 2023 the Court of Arbitration for Sport annulled the ban; FIFA appealed to the Swiss Federal Tribunal in March 2023 (outcome not checked). Human Rights Watch said witnesses and survivors had faced threats and intimidation. He has not been convicted by any court.

title: Whyte Review — British Gymnastics
who: British Gymnastics
what: Anne Whyte QC's independent review of British Gymnastics, published in June 2022 and covering August 2008 to August 2020, received more than 400 submissions (133 from current and former gymnasts) and conducted 190 interviews. More than 40% of submissions described physical abuse by coaches and more than 50% emotional abuse; more than 25% referred to excessive weight management; some 30 submissions included allegations of sexual abuse, such as sexual assault, inappropriate touching and kissing as a punishment.

title: Wrestling Federation of India — Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh (minor's complaint closed)
who: Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh (BJP MP, WFI president)
what: After months of protests by India's top wrestlers from January 2023, Delhi Police registered two FIRs against Wrestling Federation of India chief and BJP MP Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh on 28 April 2023: one under the child-protection POCSO Act for a minor wrestler, and one for six adult wrestlers, who accused him of molesting and groping them at camps and tournaments. On 27 May 2025 a Delhi court accepted a police report recommending that the minor's case be cancelled, clearing him in that case. He still faces sexual harassment and stalking charges brought by the six adult wrestlers (adults are outside this map's scope). He has always denied the allegations.

title: Bibbiano ('Angeli e Demoni') — investigation into unlawful removal of children
who: Val d'Enza social services; mayor Andrea Carletti (house arrest 2019)
what: In June 2019 Reggio Emilia prosecutors announced the 'Angeli e Demoni' investigation into Val d'Enza social services, alleging that children were wrongly removed from their families and placed in foster care on the basis of falsified reports; Bibbiano's mayor Andrea Carletti was placed under house arrest (confirmed in August 2019). Psychotherapist Claudio Foti was convicted at a fast-track trial but acquitted on appeal, and Italy's Court of Cassation confirmed his acquittal in June 2023. Carletti was acquitted in October 2024. On 9 July 2025 the Reggio Emilia court acquitted 11 of the remaining 14 defendants, many because 'the fact does not exist', and gave three light suspended sentences, the longest two years for the former head of social services. The case fits the 'adoption' setting more naturally.

title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.
what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.

title: Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days
who: Playpen (Tor site; administrator Steven W. Chase, convicted)
cover_up: After seizing the server the FBI kept Playpen running from 19 February to 4 March 2015 under a court warrant and used malware (a 'Network Investigative Technique') to unmask users; the EFF criticised the operation as continued distribution, and the 11th Circuit (2019) held the warrant invalid but did not exclude the evidence (good-faith exception). In 2017 the FBI dropped charges against one defen
what: Playpen operated on Tor from August 2014 to March 2015 and had over 215,000 users (Europol: more than 150,000) at shutdown. The FBI arrested the administrator and ran the site itself for about two weeks, unmasking users with a hacking tool. The operation led to 956 arrests of users; Europol reported 368 suspects arrested or convicted in Europe alone by May 2017. The lead administrator was sentenced to 30 years in May 2017; two co-administrators got 20 years each.

title: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cover_up: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.
what: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.

title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

title: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
what: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.

title: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
what: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

title: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months
who: Childs Play (Tor forum; owner Benjamin Faulkner, convicted)
cover_up: Queensland Police Task Force Argos operated the site for about 11 months (2016–2017), impersonating the owner and posting abuse images to keep users' trust; a UNICEF Norway legal adviser and Amnesty International criticised this, ECPAT supported it, and a York University criminologist called the server move to Australia 'jurisdiction shopping'.
what: Childs Play launched on Tor on 15 April 2016 and, with over a million registered profiles, was described as the largest site of its kind. Its Canadian administrator, Benjamin Faulkner, was arrested in Virginia in early October 2016 with American Patrick Falte; in September 2017 a federal judge in Virginia sentenced both to life for sexually abusing a toddler, and in August 2019 both received 35 years for running a child exploitation enterprise on the related Giftbox Exchange site. Australia's Task Force Argos then ran Childs Play for 11 months, until September 2017, as part of Operation Artemis, to identify victims and offenders.

title: Elysium darknet platform
who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
what: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

title: Boystown darknet platform
who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

title: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
what: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.

title: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
cover_up: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.
what: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram chatrooms; at least 10,000 people used the 'Doctor's Room' chats, some paying up to $1,200. At least 74 victims, including 16 minors, were exploited there. After petitions signed by millions, police named the operator, Cho Ju-bin, in March 2020 — the first official identity disclosure for a sex offender in South Korea — and on 26 November 2020 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to 40 years (reported raised to 42 years on appeal in 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, who created the original 'Nth Room' chatrooms, was sentenced to 34 years by the Andong court on 8 April 2021. The law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.

title: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
what: In August 2024 a journalist's reporting revealed Telegram chatrooms, some dedicated to specific high schools and middle schools, where users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female students, teachers and others; one room for pupils at a single school had more than 2,000 members. Within a week activists had identified more than 500 schools and universities as targets. Police said they had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024 by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, and that most victims and perpetrators were teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possessing or watching sexual deepfakes; earlier that month police opened an investigation into whether Telegram was complicit.

title: Scale of Harm — prevalence of livestreamed abuse in the Philippines (IJM / Rights Lab)
who: Family members and neighbours paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse
network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
what: IJM and the University of Nottingham Rights Lab estimated the prevalence of trafficking to produce child sexual exploitation material in the Philippines. IJM states that 1 in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022, that the median victim age in its earlier 2020 study was 11, average abuse lasted two years, and 9% of victims were 3 or younger. IJM UK says the UK is among the top three consumer countries.

title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

title: AUSTRAC v Westpac — payments linked to child exploitation in the Philippines
who: Westpac Banking Corporation (failure to monitor transfers)
network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
what: In November 2019 AUSTRAC alleged Westpac had breached anti-money-laundering law more than 23 million times, including failing to report international funds transfer instructions worth more than A$11 billion; the breaches included failures over suspicious transactions associated with possible child exploitation. The scandal forced the resignation of chief executive Brian Hartzer. On 24 September 2020 Westpac and AUSTRAC agreed a record A$1.3 billion penalty, the largest in Australian corporate history.

title: Australian man directed abuse of two children in the Philippines over Skype
who: Australian offender paying the children's mother
network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
what: In 2016 Task Force Argos executed a warrant at a 58-year-old Australian man's home. Using Skype he conducted 'live remote' sexual abuse of two children in the Philippines, aged two and seven when it began, while paying their mother; it continued for nearly five years. He pleaded guilty to charges including having sex with a child under 16 outside Australia.

title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
network: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

title: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
what: Men in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts, posing as a girl, to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. A federal grand jury indicted the brothers in November 2022; they were extradited from Nigeria in August 2023. The indictment said they tried to extort more than 100 people. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to sexually exploit teenage boys (announced 10 April 2024) and were each sentenced to 17.5 years in September 2024. A third defendant, Ezekiel Robert, appealed a Nigerian extradition order; charges against him remain pending.

title: Romanian man jailed for sextortion linked to a Northern Ireland teenager's suicide
who: Individual offender posing as a girl online
what: A 17-year-old from Coalisland took his own life in June 2015 after a man posing as a girl tricked him into sharing intimate images and blackmailed him. After a joint PSNI–Romanian Police investigation supported by Europol and the NCA, a 31-year-old Romanian was sentenced in Timișoara in 2017 to four years for blackmail and producing and distributing indecent images of a child.

title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

title: CVLT — neo-Nazi child exploitation group leaders arrested
who: CVLT (part of 'The Com')
what: On 30 January 2025 US HSI arrested two men for participating in CVLT, which groomed and coerced at least 16 minors worldwide into producing abuse material and self-harm imagery. Europol said earlier-arrested members included one in French custody since 2022 and one serving a 50-year US sentence. Europol describes these communities as part of 'The Com'.

title: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

title: A.M. v. Omegle — site shut after child exploitation lawsuit
who: Omegle (random video chat)
what: A plaintiff known in court documents as A.M., paired at age 11 on Omegle with an adult man who then sexually exploited her for three years (he was jailed for eight years in Canada), filed a lawsuit in November 2021 alleging the site paired minors with predators; she had sought $22 million at a jury trial. BBC reported Omegle had been mentioned in more than 50 cases against paedophiles in the previous couple of years. On 8 November 2023 founder Leif K-Brooks announced the site's closure; under an out-of-court settlement for an undisclosed sum, which A.M. said included closure, he added the line 'I thank A.M. for opening my eyes to the human cost of Omegle' with a link to the lawsuit.

title: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
who: Telegram (messaging platform)
what: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

title: US state lawsuits against Roblox and Discord over child exploitation (alleged)
who: Roblox Corporation; Discord Inc.
what: From 2025 US state attorneys general sued Roblox alleging it failed to protect children from predators, starting with Louisiana on 14 August 2025, whose attorney general called the platform 'the perfect place for pedophiles'; Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, Tennessee, Florida and Nebraska pursued similar claims, and in 2026 some states also sued Discord. In April 2026 Roblox began settling: Nevada (about $10–12 million), then Alabama ($12.2 million) and West Virginia ($11 million) on 21 April, with Roblox agreeing to age checks for all users by facial age estimation or government ID and other chat restrictions. These are allegations, not findings.

title: NCMEC: 6.9 million fewer Facebook reports after Messenger encryption
who: Meta (Facebook Messenger default end-to-end encryption)
what: NCMEC reported that CyberTipline reports fell from 36.2 million in 2023 to 20.5 million in 2024 (29.2 million incidents after adjusting for 'bundling'). It attributed part of the fall to Meta's default end-to-end encryption in Facebook Messenger (December 2023 to summer 2024), with 6.9 million fewer reports from Facebook, and to Google, X, Discord, Microsoft and Synchronoss reporting 20% fewer. NCMEC says the drop came even though the 2024 REPORT Act added mandatory reporting of enticement and child sex trafficking.

title: Apple cancels iCloud Photos CSAM scanning plan
who: Apple Inc.
what: In August 2021 Apple announced a plan to scan photos stored in iCloud for known child sexual abuse material on users' devices. After criticism from privacy and security researchers it paused the plan, and on 7 December 2022 told Wired it had decided not to move forward with the CSAM detection tool for iCloud Photos, focusing instead on its opt-in 'Communication Safety' features for children's accounts. Wikipedia reports that Apple had scanned iCloud Mail attachments for abuse imagery since 2019.

title: EU Child Sexual Abuse Regulation ('chat control') and interim derogation
who: European Commission, Council and Parliament
what: The Commission proposed the CSA Regulation (COM(2022) 209) to require platforms to assess risks and allow detection orders; it has been deadlocked over mandatory scanning. The interim derogation from the ePrivacy Directive (Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, in force 2 August 2021, extended in 2024) let providers voluntarily detect abuse material; with no agreement it lapsed on 3 April 2026. A new temporary derogation, Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, was adopted on 24 July 2026 and published 28 July 2026. As of October 2026 the permanent regulation has not been adopted.

title: UK Online Safety Act 2023
who: UK Parliament / Ofcom
what: The Online Safety Act 2023 received royal assent on 26 October 2023. It provides for the regulation by Ofcom of certain internet services, including their handling of illegal content such as child sexual abuse material and content harmful to children. Its child-protection duties, including age checks for sites with certain adult content, came into force in late July 2025.

title: US Kids Online Safety Act, EARN IT Act and REPORT Act
who: US Congress
what: The EARN IT Act, which would condition platforms' liability shield on child-safety practices, was introduced in 2020, 2022 and 2023 and died in committee. The Kids Online Safety Act passed the Senate 91–3 on 30 July 2024 but did not pass the House that Congress; it was reintroduced in May 2025, and in June 2026 the House Energy and Commerce Committee reportedly agreed a revised version. The REPORT Act, passed in 2024, expanded platforms' mandatory reporting to NCMEC to include online enticement and child sex trafficking and raised fines for failing to report; NCMEC attributed a jump in child sex trafficking reports, from 5,976 in the first half of 2024 to 62,891 in the first half of 2025, to the law. The TAKE IT DOWN Act was signed in May 2025.

title: Australia: eSafety Commissioner, Online Safety Act 2021 and under-16 social media ban
who: Office of the eSafety Commissioner
what: Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 (Act No. 76 of 2021) gives the eSafety Commissioner removal and transparency powers over online services. On 28 November 2024 parliament approved a ban on children under 16 using social media, to be enforced by the eSafety regulator with fines of up to A$50 million for non-compliant companies, taking effect at least 12 months later. Wikipedia reports that Roblox, initially excluded, was to be covered by protocols from March 2026, and that in June 2020 Australia passed the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Sexual Crimes Against Children and Community Protection Measures) Act, which IJM said recognised Australians' role in demand for livestreamed abuse.

title: Stanford finds abuse material links in LAION-5B AI training dataset
who: LAION-5B dataset (German non-profit LAION)
what: In December 2023 a Stanford Internet Observatory study found 3,226 suspected instances of child sexual abuse material in LAION-5B, a dataset used to train Stable Diffusion and other image generators, 1,008 of them externally validated. LAION, the German non-profit that created it, temporarily took down LAION-5B and LAION-400M to check them before republishing. NCMEC has reported that its 2025 CyberTipline data included more than 12,000 reports involving CSAM found in AI training data.

title: Grok image tool used to sexualise photos of minors (alleged)
who: X Corp / xAI (Grok)
what: After X rolled out an 'edit image' button for its Grok chatbot in late December 2025, users complained that it was being used to partially or completely remove clothing from pictures of women and children. On 2 January 2026 Grok posted that it had 'identified lapses in safeguards' and was 'urgently fixing them', adding that CSAM is illegal and prohibited; xAI replied to AFP with an automated message saying 'the mainstream media lies'. In August 2026 a plaintiff ('Jane Doe') sued, alleging Grok was trained on abuse material of her and that the Canadian Centre for Child Protection had found Grok-generated AI CSAM depicting her. NCMEC listed X.AI LLC among companies most of whose CyberTipline reports lacked enough information to locate offences, while noting improvements in early 2026. These are allegations.

title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.
what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

title: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
who: Blue Orchid website
what: A Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. The investigation began in May 2000 when Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help; Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By 26 March 2001 US Customs announced that four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, with customers arrested in California, New York and Indiana and leads passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.

title: LS Models / 'Alex Model' raids, Ukraine
who: 'Alex Model' agency (LS-Models brands)
cover_up: Despite surveillance and arrests the legal outcome was described as lenient.
what: A Kyiv modelling agency with branches in Kharkiv and Simferopol recruited children through TV, newspaper and radio adverts and produced sexualised images sold worldwide under 'LS' brands from 2001. Police raided it in July 2004; at the same time over 150 people were arrested in Australia for possession and distribution.

title: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
cover_up: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.
what: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.

title: 'Kids the Light of our Lives' forum
who: Online chat forum with live streaming of abuse
what: An internet chat room, hosted from Buxhall in Suffolk, featuring images and live streams of the sexual abuse of children. Forensic teams found 75,960 indecent images on the host's computer and evidence he had supplied 11,491 images to other users. The trail began in Canada with the arrest of 24 offenders; in a 10-month operation by the Virtual Global Taskforce, led by the UK's CEOP and involving agencies from 35 countries, officers posed as the host and ran the chat room for 10 days. British authorities said on 18 June 2007 that more than 700 suspects had been identified worldwide and 31 children rescued, some only a few months old. The host, Timothy David Martyn Cox, admitted nine counts of possessing and distributing indecent images and was given an indeterminate sentence at Ipswich Crown Court that day.

title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.
what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.

title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

title: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
what: A year-long global investigation into the Tor child-abuse site 'Babyheart' and its administrator involved the UK NCA and West Midlands Police, Australian Federal Police and Queensland's Task Force Argos, Toronto Police, the Brazilian Federal Police, INTERPOL, Europol and US ICE, with nine countries listed (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Portugal, the US and the UK). Intelligence narrowed the administrator's location to Portugal, where the Portuguese Judicial Police arrested and charged him in 2017; examination of his devices identified seven victims directly related to him. INTERPOL and Portuguese police presented the case publicly on 23 January 2020. Brazil's Federal Police ran related 'Operação Lobos' phases.

title: DarkScandals site administrator arrested
who: DarkScandals (dark and clear web site)
what: A site on both the dark and clear web that advertised rape and blackmail videos of girls and included child abuse material (over 2,000 videos and images). After US IRS-CI, HSI and DOJ, Dutch police and FIOD, the BKA and Europol cooperated, Dutch police arrested the administrator at his home in Barendrecht on 9 March 2020 and the site was taken down.

title: Operation Gargamel — Belgian-led investigation of 9 million files
who: Offenders producing their own abuse material
what: Belgian federal judicial police found more than 9 million images and videos, mostly never seen before, in a house search. With Europol victim-identification taskforces, 90 suspects (24 in Belgium) and 110 victims were identified by March 2020; an Australian suspect was sentenced to 15 years. Police in over 40 countries received intelligence packages.

title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

title: Operation Tantalio — WhatsApp groups sharing abuse material
who: 25 invitation-only WhatsApp groups linked from Tor
what: Spanish National Police found Tor users being directed to invitation-only WhatsApp groups (25 under investigation). Action days on 28–29 March 2017 with Europol and Interpol led to 39 arrests in Europe and South America; more than 100 targets in 13 Central and South American countries were pursued through Interpol.

title: Operation Chemosh — minors sharing abuse 'stickers' in WhatsApp groups
who: Encrypted chat groups, many members minors
what: Begun in 2017 after a public report about children forming WhatsApp groups to create and exchange abuse material, including emoji 'stickers'. Thirty-three investigations were opened (26 in Spain) with arrests in Spain, Italy and France; the average age of those arrested in Spain was 22 because many were minors.

title: Tbilisi photo studio producing abuse material for foreign buyers
who: Photo studio owners and foreign clients
what: Georgian police, with Australian and US authorities and Europol, arrested 11 members of a group including studio owners and American and Australian citizens who arranged the production of sexual images of girls aged 8 to 14 in rented apartments in Tbilisi. Some girls were abused with parental consent in exchange for 500–3,000 GEL (about €150–900).

title: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
what: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.
